Andrei Tarkovsky during the first filming period in Estonia. He was 45 and often wore a denim suit on set.
Evening filming relied largely on the remaining natural light, shaped with large black cloths and, for close-ups, a small light below the actors’ faces.
The first filming period used a Mitchell NC camera and fast Distagon lenses, with the aperture fully open for the low-light conditions.

For the resumed production, Alexander Knyazhinsky became director of photography and most scenes were filmed on a Soviet KCN camera with a Cooke Varotal zoom lens.
The second filming period in Estonia began with the heroes arriving in the Zone, stopping the handcar and continuing on foot.
For the distant military landscape, real and fabricated equipment was combined while a pyrotechnician used a smoke float to create fog according to the wind.
The shot of the Stalker lying in a shallow canal was filmed in cold water; Nelly Fomina devised a waterproof, insulated diving suit beneath the actor’s costume.
Rails were laid on either side of the actor so the camera dolly could straddle him, with its wheels divided between the two tracks.
The camera, mounted at the edge of the dolly and aimed downward, passed over the actor during a carefully timed three-minute move.
Tarkovsky was closely involved in filming and rehearsal and often took the cinematographer’s position behind the camera.
Tarkovsky also worked closely with the decorators, attending to the smallest details and jokingly asking them to “make an ikebana.”

Rashit Safiullin, a production designer from Kazan, was an indefatigable assistant in preparing each shot.
During a cold-weather rehearsal, Anatoly Solonitsyn lay on wet moss surrounded by water, as the scene required.

A soft-focus portrait of a smiling Tarkovsky, made after he recognized the photographer’s old Voigtländer as the same kind of camera his father had owned.
Close-ups for the passage into the Zone used actors on a railway platform while an Arriflex with a Steadicam moved beside them on a separate dolly track.
During a Land Rover and locomotive setup, crossed signals between Tarkovsky, the driver and assistant Eugene Tsymbal repeatedly sent the locomotive off too early.
